en: The Origin of Dance:
A dance-drama composed by Śrī Suvrahmaṇya Dīkṣita,
titled *Nṛtyaprasūti*.
Always worship with a sweet mind the conqueror of Māra, who is the primordial joy, the essence of the earth, and the beginning of all things.
I bow to the one who possesses compassion, who is easily pleased, the enemy of desire, and the subduer of the elephant;
who ferries beings across the terrible ocean of existence; whose pair of feet is like the rising sun;
the sovereign of yogis, the turner of the wheel of Dharma.

The King of the Gods, overcome with intense devotion, approaches the first object of vision: [the Buddha] seated at the foot of a tree, surrounded by disciples, whose flower of wisdom is in full bloom.
He whose voice is like a swan, who is terrifying at the beginning [of creation], who wields the vajra weapon,
and who is the glorious moon among kings— this is he.
Then, after a short time, the heroic King of the Gods, Indra—eager for the splendor of the hundred-gated city—having become victorious, dances a dance of victory, exclaiming:
"I have become victorious! I have become victorious!"
Then, suddenly emerging from the ear, the Tripura Asuras terrified the gods with showers of various weapons. Overcome by fear, the gods prayed to the Supreme Lord.
[The rest of the passage begins with: "Darbha, etc."

Harassed by the terrifying forms of Tripura, we, filled with fear, have taken refuge in the self-born Śambhunātha, the supreme Śiva who is not terrible (Aghora). With palms joined in reverence and intense devotion, we cry out "O Bhava! O Śiva! and pray to him.
On the stage of the dance, the night appears like darkness for even a single moment; then, seeing the arrival of Śiva, the gods sing.
Then Maheśvara, shining with intense splendor, arrived at Nāṭakarunji,
his two hands free of weapons and surrounded by a host of Maruts.
And with a roar accompanied by a cry of "ca," for the destruction of all enemies,
O God of Gods, requested thus by Vāk, Deva, Vaikuṇṭha, and the others, quickly [protect] us according to the scriptures!
O Lord who are beyond passion and beyond counting,
now all the gods sing [your praises],
ever prepared for victory in battle; we, being unobstructed, exceedingly capable, and having taken refuge in Tryambaka, [remain steadfast].
I am one whose speed is like that of an arrow released from the hand; I am skilled in shattering [all things].
(ca 3) O Lord, I am endowed with unsurpassed velocity; I am skilled at uprooting [all things], merciless, and most piercing. (ca 4) I am eager to torment those who possess incomparable power.
I am one whose curved nose resembles the incomparable trunk of an elephant;
I am known by the name Vināka, the preeminent archer; I am the bearer of the sovereign of bowmen, fierce and adorned with a bowstring that produces a sound terrifying to the Dānavas.
And I, armed with a trident of vajra-essence, skilled in piercing the bodies of enemies, shall bring my foes under my control by means of a velocity beyond the reach of words;
then all the gods and Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess, circumambulate me, exulting in victory in battle.
Thus singing,
the host of gods, led by Pañcavaṭī and others, beheld him who bore the mark of "mine-ness" (mamatā) and heard his manifestation of prowess.
Thinking that the burning of Tripura and the seizing of Mamatā were simultaneous acts of the gods,
the daughter of Himavat, her senses conquered, beheld the smiling face of Śambhu;
and seeing his beautiful countenance marked by a gentle laugh, she was pierced by the moon-crested Lord’s arrow.
Marked by the sentiments of joy and wrath, he suddenly let out a great laugh, like the sound of hundreds of millions of kettledrums at the destruction of Tripura; it occurred at that very moment.
This is the second vision.
A short time later, at the hour of dusk on Mount Kailāsa, all the gods assembled to witness the dance of the Supreme Lord. Śambhu proceeds to perform the dance.
At the onset of dusk, the immortals offer praise to the Supreme Lord, who is intent upon his dance.

Having observed Śambhu, who was filled with enthusiasm by the playing of the *tūṃburu* lute, the *ānanda* lute, and the *mṛdaṅga* drum— his vow being maintained, his movements neither slow nor hurried, but even and steady— the lotus-faced daughter of Himavat looked at him with a smile.

When Nārada requested with soft words from her pair of jar-like breasts, the sage sang the nectar of his song, which resembled the bimba fruit; then the sage Nārada sang the story of the Destroyer of Tripura.

Kāmbodhi, terrified and tormented by the formidable, most cruel, and death-dealing Tripura, the lord of the Asuras, sought refuge in Tryambaka along with Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and all the hosts of gods. "O Abode of Mercy, O Supreme Lord, protect us! he entreated. His inner being rippled with compassion, Śaṅkara, the bestower of fearlessness who is himself weaponless, immediately became intent on the destruction of Tripura.
The gods then prayed to him: "Make us righteous according to the scriptures."
"O King, I shall become a bow," "I shall become an arrow," "I shall become a trident"— proclaiming these words loudly,
they dance like conquerors of the elements. Having seen them...
Urged by the arising of the sentiment of laughter marked by the flavor of compassion,
Maheśvara let out a loud, great laugh; at that very moment, the Bhūtas, beholding the burning of Tripura, had their eyes wide with amazement.
The gods utter cries of "Hāhā! and sing praises;
Śambhu displays all of this through gestures at the conclusion of the song, while Śaṅkara proclaims it with enthusiasm.
"Behold, this new treatise marked by the name 'Abhinaya' has been created! Then Śambhu called upon Taṇḍu and sang and danced, manifesting the nine rasas and so forth.

Listen to me, O great sage: this new treatise has been composed by me and is marked with the name *Abhinaya*. It should be propagated by teachers; it is said that *nṛtya* (dramatic dance) is characterized by *abhinaya* (gestural representation), while *nṛtta* (pure dance) is not so marked.
Protect this [work], which is marked by the nine rasas like the two eyes of Locanā;
may there be a *tāṇḍava* dance marked by manliness,
and may I become its instructor upon the earth through that *Tāṇḍu*.
Having spoken thus, the dance of feminine nature marked by the name *lāsya* should be performed by the two women; then, urged by Pārvatī, Śambhu shall dance,
and then all shall dance.
We worship Śambhu,
the Lord with matted hair, who has cast away the entire multitude of all sins,
by means of dances, gestures, and joyful performances of both *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava*.
Here, with dances that resound like the roar of thunder, we worship Śambhu— who is marked by the seven *tālas* beginning with *śrī-sūla*— as well as the Mountain-Maiden (Pārvatī),
who is adorned with garlands of *kiṅkirāta* flowers, using skull-bowls as vessels.
And [he saw her] resting upon the earth, displaying compassion and a most peaceful yoga for the destruction of the asuras; she manifested heroic, fierce, and other moods,
while revealing a full erotic sentiment with her body bowed low.
We also bow to Bhavānī, who embraces Bhava in her middle, and to Bhava himself; we bow to Gaṅgādhara, who censures the speakers of doubt,
and to her who dances amidst the rivaling heroines such as Kalahāntaritā and Khaṇḍitā.
I worship the woman who has her husband under her control, who is adorned for her tryst at the doorway, whose nose-ornament jingles with a loud sound, and who intoxicates Śaṅkara.
